title: Like ‘family businesses’: Inside the Nvidia board that ousted and rehired Jensen Huang | CNN Business
text:
Source: CNN

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang gushed last year that support from longtime board members Tench Coxe, Mark Stevens and Harvey Jones was crucial to helping him navigate three decades of running the company.

“They not one time gave up on the company and us,” Huangtold the Acquired podcastof the board members and other early employees.

Those same supporters have now helped see Huang through his biggest challenge yet — restoring his role as CEO following an unprecedented corporate scandal. But their close relationships have alsoraised questionsabout the board’s independence and whether it was equipped to hold Huang accountable and protect shareholders’ interests.

Including Huang, nearly half of Nvidia’s 11-person board has been with the company since its early days. Its three longest-serving members — Coxe, Stevens and Jones — saw the value of their combined holdings in the company jump by nearly $2.5 billion from Friday to Monday, after Huang was brought back.

His reinstatement marks a sharp turnaround from a week ago, when Jones said the board had unanimously accepted Huang’s resignation, and had no intention of bringing him back. And it comes despite Huang’s relationship with a woman that US officials feared could be a Chinese intelligence asset, as well as multiple reports about an extramarital affair with a subordinate.President Donald Trump has also been open about his role in pushing the board to give Huang his job back.

“The appearance of the relationship between the board and Jensen is most akin to family businesses that go public — that’s a domain in which it’s not uncommon for directors to be there for a long time,” said Jo-Ellen Pozner, management professor at Santa Clara University’s Leavey School of Business. “But those kinds of companies are not major players in the global economy.”

Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, the Yale professor known as the “CEO Whisperer,” onMonday calledthe Nvidia board’s decision to reinstate Huang a “complete failure of corporate governance” and urged them to resign.

Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment on this story.

Aside from Huang, whose board seat was restored along with his CEO title, four members of Nvidia’s board have been with the company for around three decades.

That includes Jones, who was named last week as Nvidia’s first-ever board chair after joining the company at its inception in 1993. At the time, he’d been serving as CEO of software firm Synopsys, where Nvidia’s original founders had been customers before they approached Jones to bring his operational expertise to the board of their new company.

Coxe and Stevens, early Nvidia investors, have also served on the board since 1993, although Stevens took a two-year hiatus from 2006 to 2008. Brooke Seawell, who previously worked alongside Jones at Synopsys, joined Nvidia’s board in 1997.

Having long tenured board members means having a “longstanding mission and espirit de corps that a lot of people pointed to as a source of strength for the company,” said Eric Talley, professor at Columbia Law School and co-host of the Beyond Unprecedented podcast. But “it does set up situations where a board might be very, very reluctant to exercise real oversight over someone who’s now become their old friend and someone who has given them loyalty over the years.”

That may be why, for example, the board had been reluctant to challenge Huang’s opposition to succession planning that left them flat-footed, causing investors to panic when news of his affairs and concerns about national security riskcame to light.

Even many of the board members who have joined, by Nvidia’s standards, more recently, have, by current, typical corporate governance standards, been there a relatively long time.

Research on corporate boards suggests that the “maximum efficacy” of a board member peaks around eight to 10 years and then “trails off dramatically,” Pozner said.

“Boards that have longer tenures are referred to as zombie boards,” she said, “because the implication is that people then are asleep at the wheel in terms of their ability to engage in active oversight because they become like insiders.”

Still, Talley noted that when it came to reinstating Huang, the board was in a difficult position: stick with their original decision to move on without Huang and risk angering some of their biggest customers and the president “who can wield a fairly heavy governmental and regulatory hammer.” Or it couldreverse course, which “makes the board look weaker,” and puts them at risk if additional issues arise from the ongoing internal, state and federal investigations.

Going forward, the board may be mindful of keeping a tight leash on Huang to ensure it doesn’t look ineffective, Talley said. It appointed its newest member, Suzanne Nora Johnson, the retired vice chair of Goldman Sachs who joined Nvidia in May, to lead the National Security and Export Controls Oversight Committee it created last week amid the scandal.

Nvidia’s longtime board members also stood to gain financially from Huang’s return. Jones, Coxe and Stevens together own more than 62 million shares in the company, according to data compiled by FactSet based on the most recent filings to the Securities and Exchange Commission. The combined value of their holdings declined by nearly $5 billion from the end of October, before the Huang debacle began, through Friday, before making up around half of those losses Monday when Haung’s return boosted the stock by more than 30%.

It is typical for corporate board members to own stock in the company; it aligns their interests with those of the shareholders they represent. Nvidia’s board may have decided that, like for them, Huang’s return was in the best interest of all shareholders given the dramatic decline in the stock price following his exit.

However, experts say significant holdings could lead to short-term decision making. Nvidia’s longtime board members have all seen their personal wealth rise dramatically in recent years as the company’s valuation skyrocketed.

“Now you’re an insider to that company, your portfolio starts to take on the look of an employee’s portfolio,” Pozner said. “It’s impossible then to separate yourself from the company in a way that allows you to maintain the kind of distance that board independence is supposed to ensure.”
